How would you fine-tune an LLM using LoR: LoRA/QLoRA freeze the base model's weights and train small low-rank adapter matrices injected into attention layers, so you get most of the benefit of fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory and compute cost (QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization of the base model to fine-tune large models on a single GPU). Fine-tuning is worth it when you need to change the model's style/format/behavior consistently across every call, or teach it a narrow skill it can't reliably do via prompting (e.g. strict output schemas, a domain-specific tone, or a classification task) - not when the problem is missing knowledge, which RAG solves more cheaply and with easier updates. A common production pattern is RAG for facts plus a lightweight fine-tune for behavior/format, since the two solve different problems and are not mutually exclusive.
How would you design an evaluation pipel: Build a versioned golden dataset of representative inputs with expected properties (not always one exact answer - often a rubric), and run every prompt/model/RAG change through it before deploy: automated metrics where possible (exact match, retrieval recall, JSON schema validity), an LLM-as-judge step scoring subjective qualities like helpfulness or faithfulness against the rubric, and periodic human review sampling to catch what the judge model misses or is biased on. Treat this exactly like a test suite in CI - a prompt or model change that regresses the eval score should block deployment - and keep the golden set growing with real production failures you've seen, so evaluation reflects actual failure modes rather than only the cases you imagined up front.
What guardrail frameworks or techniques: For structured output, use constrained decoding/JSON mode where the provider supports it, or validate every response against a schema (Pydantic/JSON Schema) and retry with an error message fed back to the model on failure rather than trusting free-text parsing. For safety, layer input guardrails (classify/block prompt injection, PII, and disallowed topics before the request reaches the model), output guardrails (a second pass or a framework like NeMo Guardrails/Llama Guard checking the response before it reaches the user), and business-logic guardrails (never let the model directly execute a high-risk action - route it through the same approval and validation path a human-triggered action would go through).
How would you choose chunk size and over: Start from the content's natural structure - chunk along semantic boundaries (sections, paragraphs, code blocks) rather than a fixed character count where possible, since splitting mid-thought hurts retrieval quality more than chunk size alone. A typical starting point is a few hundred tokens per chunk with 10-20% overlap so an answer that spans a chunk boundary isn't lost, but the only way to actually validate the choice is empirically: run your evaluation set (question -> expected source chunk) against a few chunk-size/overlap combinations and measure retrieval recall directly, rather than picking a number from a blog post and hoping.
How would you manage context window and: For long conversations, don't send the full history forever - summarize older turns into a compact running summary once the conversation exceeds a threshold, keep the last few turns verbatim for recency, and only re-inject retrieved context relevant to the current turn rather than the entire document. For large documents, chunk and retrieve relevant sections via RAG instead of stuffing the whole document into context, and track actual token usage per request so you can alert before a conversation silently starts truncating important early context or blowing through cost/latency budgets.
How would you design prompt caching to r: Use provider-level prompt/context caching (e.g. caching a long, repeated system prompt or document context so only the new user turn is billed/re-processed at full cost) for requests that share a large common prefix, and add an application-level response cache (keyed on a normalized version of the full prompt) for genuinely repeated queries like FAQ-style questions. Be explicit about invalidation - cached responses tied to a document or policy must be invalidated when that source changes - and monitor cache hit rate as a first-class metric, since a low hit rate means the caching strategy doesn't match real traffic patterns and isn't earning its complexity.
How would you curate and validate a fine: Curate for diversity and correctness over raw volume: deduplicate near-identical examples, balance the distribution of categories/intents so the model doesn't overfit to whatever was easiest to collect, and have a human review pass (or a strong LLM-as-judge pass) on a sample to catch labeling errors before they get baked into the model. Validate by fine-tuning and running the full evaluation suite (not just the fine-tuning task's own metric) to check for regressions on unrelated capabilities, and hold out a slice of the fine-tuning data itself as a test set to confirm the model actually learned the intended pattern rather than memorizing.
How would you design multi-tenant rate l: Issue each team a scoped API key/service account with a token-per-minute and requests-per-minute quota enforced at a gateway layer in front of the model provider, so one team's traffic spike can't starve others - this is the same bulkhead pattern used for any shared internal service. For chargeback, log token usage (prompt + completion tokens) per request tagged with team/project, aggregate it into a cost dashboard or a BigQuery table, and set budget alerts per team so a runaway job or misconfigured retry loop gets caught in hours, not at the next monthly bill.
A model provider announces they are depr: Treat it like any dependency upgrade with a hard deadline: run the full evaluation suite against the new model version well before the deprecation date to quantify behavior differences (some prompts that worked well on the old model may need rewriting, since prompting is not perfectly portable across model versions), and roll out via canary/shadow traffic comparing old-vs-new model outputs on real requests before fully cutting over. Keep the model identifier abstracted behind a config value (never hardcoded inline) so the actual cutover is a config change gated by the eval results, not a code change under deadline pressure.
What data security risks exist when fine: The core risks are the fine-tuned model memorizing and later regurgitating sensitive training examples verbatim (a real risk with small fine-tuning sets), and the training data pipeline itself becoming a new place secrets/PII can leak (logs, intermediate storage, third-party fine-tuning APIs). Mitigate with PII/secret scrubbing before data ever enters the training set, testing the fine-tuned model for memorization by probing with near-duplicates of training examples, keeping fine-tuning data and jobs inside the same security boundary (VPC, IAM scope) as other sensitive data, and preferring providers/regions that contractually guarantee your data isn't used to train their base models.
How would you design memory for an agent: Short-term memory is the current conversation/task's working context - recent turns, tool results, and the current plan - kept in the prompt directly since it's small and immediately relevant. Long-term memory is anything that should persist across sessions (user preferences, past decisions, learned facts) and belongs in an external store (a vector database for semantic recall, or a structured store for facts with clear keys) that the agent queries via a retrieval tool call rather than holding in context permanently. The design discipline is deciding what's worth remembering at all - unbounded memory growth degrades retrieval quality and increases cost, so most production agents summarize or expire old memories rather than keeping everything forever.
How would you design a multi-agent syste: The supervisor agent owns the overall plan and decomposes a task into subtasks, dispatching each to a specialized worker (e.g. a research agent, a code-writing agent, a validation agent) via a structured handoff - typically a tool call carrying the subtask description and any needed context, with the worker returning a structured result rather than free text. Keep handoffs explicit and typed (a defined schema for what a worker returns) so the supervisor can programmatically decide the next step, and give the supervisor a way to detect a worker failing or looping so it can retry, escalate to a human, or route to a different worker rather than the whole system silently stalling.
How would you prevent an agent from gett: Set a hard max-iteration/max-tool-call limit per task as a non-negotiable circuit breaker, track cumulative token spend per run and abort if it crosses a budget threshold, and detect repetition explicitly (the same tool called with the same or near-identical arguments more than once or twice is a strong loop signal worth failing fast on rather than letting it continue). Log every iteration so a human can see exactly where a stuck run went wrong, and prefer failing loudly with a clear error over silently truncating - a capped-but-visible failure is far easier to debug and fix than a run that quietly produced a degraded partial result.
How would you test and evaluate an agent: Run the change against a fixed suite of representative task scenarios (a superset of real user tasks and known edge cases/failure modes previously seen in production) and score both the final outcome and the path taken to get there - two agents can reach the same answer through very different, not equally acceptable, tool-call sequences. Compare the new version's pass rate, average tool calls, and cost per task against the current production version, and treat any regression on previously-passing scenarios as a blocker, exactly like a unit test suite for traditional code, just scored by outcome/rubric instead of exact-match assertions.
What guardrails would you put around an: Classify actions by risk tier and require explicit human approval before executing anything in the high-risk tier (deletions, production deploys, financial transactions), with the agent proposing the action and its reasoning rather than executing silently. For actions that are allowed to run autonomously, prefer reversible-by-design operations (soft delete with a retention window instead of hard delete, canary rollout instead of full deploy) and hard scope limits on what the agent's credentials can even reach (least-privilege IAM, a narrow allowlist of resources), so a mistake is contained and recoverable even if the approval step is somehow bypassed.
How would you debug an agent that produc: Pull the full trace of that specific run first - the exact prompt sent, every tool call with its arguments and returned result, and the model's intermediate reasoning if captured - since the wrong action is almost always explainable by a bad tool result, a misleading piece of retrieved context, or an ambiguous instruction the model resolved incorrectly, rather than the model being arbitrarily wrong. Reproduce it with the same inputs to confirm it's a repeatable failure mode (not a one-off), then decide whether the fix belongs in the prompt, the tool's input validation, the retrieval quality, or an added guardrail - and add that exact scenario to the regression eval suite so the same failure can't silently reappear after a future change.
How would you version and roll back an a: Package the prompt, tool schemas, and the orchestration graph (LangGraph definition or equivalent) as a single versioned artifact - checked into source control together, not managed as separately-editable pieces - so a version number always refers to one coherent, reproducible configuration of the agent. Deploy through the same canary/evaluation gate used for any other change, and keep the previous version's artifact immediately available so rollback is repointing to a prior version ID, not manually reconstructing what the prompt and tools used to look like from memory or scattered edit history.
How would you simulate or replay agent r: Record full traces of real production runs (inputs, tool calls, and results) and replay them by mocking the tool layer with the recorded responses, so you can re-run the same scenario through a new prompt/model version deterministically at the orchestration level even though the LLM's own token sampling isn't deterministic. For evaluation, run each scenario multiple times (e.g. 3-5 samples) and score the distribution of outcomes rather than a single run, since a single non-deterministic pass/fail is not a reliable signal - a version that passes 5/5 is meaningfully better than one that passes 3/5 even if both technically 'passed' once.
What is AIOps, and how is it different f: Traditional monitoring/observability collects metrics, logs, and traces and lets humans set thresholds and interpret dashboards; AIOps applies machine learning on top of that same telemetry to do things humans don't scale well at - detecting anomalies without a manually-tuned static threshold, correlating hundreds of alerts into one probable incident, clustering millions of log lines into a handful of patterns, and predicting capacity issues before they happen. AIOps doesn't replace observability - it's a layer on top that reduces the human toil of watching dashboards and correlating signals manually, and it's only as good as the underlying telemetry it's fed.
How would you design anomaly detection f: A static threshold fails immediately on seasonal data (normal Monday-morning traffic looks like an 'anomaly' against a quiet Sunday-night baseline), so use a model that's seasonality-aware - comparing the current value against the same time-of-day/day-of-week window historically (e.g. this Tuesday 2pm vs the last 4 Tuesdays at 2pm) rather than a flat baseline, or a decomposition approach (STL/Prophet-style) that separates trend, seasonality, and residual, then flags anomalies only in the residual. Tune sensitivity against a labeled set of known-good and known-bad periods before trusting it in production, and always pair it with a minimum-duration/persistence rule (anomalous for N consecutive windows) so single-point noise doesn't page anyone.
How would you use log clustering to redu: Normalize log lines by masking variable tokens (timestamps, IDs, IP addresses, numeric values) so structurally identical messages collapse into the same template, then cluster by template frequency and recency - this alone typically reduces tens of thousands of raw lines to a few dozen distinct patterns. Surface the patterns that are new (never seen before this incident window) or whose frequency spiked sharply, since those are far more likely to be causally related to the incident than high-volume but constant background noise that was already present before things broke.
How would you design alert correlation t: Correlate on multiple signals together: time proximity (alerts firing within the same short window), topology (services connected in the dependency graph - a downstream alert is likely caused by an upstream one, not an independent issue), and known alert relationships learned from past incidents (this alert and that alert have fired together before). Group correlated alerts into a single incident with one clear primary suspect surfaced first, and route only one page to on-call for the group - with the individual alerts still visible and linked for full context - rather than a page-per-alert flood that trains people to ignore pages during real incidents.
How would you use a service dependency/t: Maintain (or auto-discover via traces/service mesh) a graph of which services call which, then when multiple services show symptoms simultaneously, rank candidate root causes by graph position - a node that is upstream of every other affected service is a stronger root-cause candidate than one that's downstream of all of them, since failures propagate along call-graph edges. Combine this with change correlation (what deployed, scaled, or config-changed on that node right before symptoms started) to turn 'probably this service' into a much higher-confidence, actionable first suspect for the on-call engineer instead of a wall of equally-weighted alerts.
How would you design safe auto-remediati: Scope auto-remediation to a narrow allowlist of well-understood, reversible actions (restart a single unhealthy pod, scale out within a pre-approved max) - never open-ended or destructive actions - and always rate-limit and circuit-break the remediation itself (e.g. don't restart the same service more than twice in ten minutes, since a persistent crash-loop needs a human, not an infinite restart cycle). Log every auto-remediation action as loudly as a human-triggered one, alert the on-call that it happened even though it didn't page them, and require a human-approved runbook behind every automated action so there's always a clear, reviewed decision trail for why the system was allowed to act autonomously in that specific case.
How would you use historical metrics to: Fit a trend model (even simple linear regression on recent history works for steady growth; use a seasonal forecasting model like Prophet for cyclical traffic) on the resource's historical usage, project forward to the point it crosses the hard limit, and alert with enough lead time to act (e.g. 'projected to hit 90% capacity in 18 days' rather than only alerting once you're already at 90%). Re-fit the forecast regularly since growth rates change, and treat a forecast crossing the threshold as a planning trigger for a human decision (provision more, optimize usage, or accept the risk) rather than something that should silently auto-provision unbounded infrastructure.
How would you decide between buying an A: Buy when you need broad, quick coverage across many services and don't have a dedicated team to maintain custom models - commercial platforms come with pre-built correlation, log clustering, and integrations that would take a real team-quarter to replicate. Build in-house when you have a narrow, high-value, well-understood signal (e.g. a specific business metric anomaly) where a simple custom model outperforms a generic product, or when data residency/cost at your scale makes a vendor platform impractical. In practice, most mature platform teams do both - a commercial AIOps layer for broad alert correlation and noise reduction, plus a few targeted custom models for their highest-value specific signals.
How would you measure whether an AIOps o: Track MTTR before and after adoption on comparable incident classes, alert volume and page-per-incident ratio (a working correlation system should reduce pages per incident, not just add another dashboard), and precision/recall on the anomaly detector specifically - what fraction of its flags were real issues (precision) and what fraction of real issues it actually caught (recall). If MTTR isn't measurably improving and alert volume isn't measurably dropping after a reasonable adoption period, that's a signal the system is adding noise or being ignored rather than earning trust, and it needs retuning or removal rather than being left running unmeasured indefinitely.
What are the failure modes of AIOps syst: The two opposite failure modes are the system crying wolf (too many false-positive anomalies, teaching engineers to ignore it, which is just alert fatigue relocated one layer up) and the system being blindly trusted (an auto-remediation or root-cause suggestion gets acted on without verification, and when it's wrong once, it's wrong at machine speed and scale). Prevent both by measuring and publishing the system's own precision/recall openly so trust is calibrated to actual performance rather than assumed, keeping a human in the loop for any high-impact action, and treating the AIOps system's own alerts and suggestions as inputs to a decision - not the decision itself - especially early in its deployment before it has an earned track record.
